segments.say: Lesson 7. Decoding: Temperature, Top-k, Top-p. How the next token is chosen, and how to tune for creativity versus determinism.

After the model scores every possible next token, decoding settings like temperature and top-p decide how it picks one: safely (most likely) or creatively (more random). Here is an analogy. Ordering at a restaurant: temperature 0 always orders the house favourite; higher temperature sometimes tries something unusual, occasionally something weird.

Why does this matter? Choosing settings per use case (extraction versus brainstorming) is everyday A I-engineering work. max tokens and stop sequences control cost and output length. A few key words. Temperature: Randomness dial: 0 equals predictable, higher equals creative. Top-p: Only sample from the most likely tokens covering p of the probability. Greedy: Always pick the top token. max tokens: Upper limit on output length.
Choosing the next token. The model outputs a probability for every token in the vocabulary. Here are the top 5.
Greedy: always pick the highest. Deterministic, but it can be bland or repetitive.
Low temperature divides the logits by a small number, so the distribution gets peakier and the top token dominates. Use it for extraction, code, classification.
High temperature flattens it: more variety, and more nonsense ("purple" now 11%). Good for brainstorming, risky for facts.
Top-k: keep only the k most likely tokens, renormalize, then sample.
Top-p: keep the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p. The set size adapts: small when the model is confident, larger when it's unsure.

The knobs. temperature: 0 about deterministic, 0.7 balanced, above 1 wild. top p: nucleus sampling, typically 0.9–1.0. top k: hard cap on candidates (not exposed by every A P I). max tokens: output length cap. Also a cost and latency guard. stop sequences: strings that end generation early. frequency / presence penalties: discourage repetition.

Practical defaults. Structured extraction, sequel, tool calls, classification: temperature 0–0.2. rag answers: 0–0.3 to stay faithful to the context. Creative writing and brainstorming: 0.7–1.0. Usually tune either temperature or top p, not both aggressively.

Gotcha: temperature 0 ≠ perfectly reproducible. Even at temperature 0, outputs can vary slightly because of G P U floating-point non-determinism and batching. For tests, use evals with tolerance, not exact string matches.

Say it in the interview. "The model outputs a distribution over the vocabulary. Temperature rescales it, and top-k or top-p truncate it before sampling. For agents and extraction I run near-zero temperature for consistency. For ideation I raise it. I always set max tokens and stop sequences for cost control.".

Let's compare. Greedy: argmax, yes (mostly), short factual outputs. Temperature: rescales logits, no (unless 0), global creativity dial. Top-k: top k candidates, no, simple cap on weirdness. Top-p (nucleus): smallest set greater than or equal to p mass, no, adaptive, the common default. Beam search: tracks several best sequences, yes, translation; rare in chat.

A likely interview question: Temperature versus top-p? A strong answer: Temperature reshapes the whole distribution (sharper or flatter). Top-p truncates it to the smallest set covering p of the probability mass. Tune one primarily.
That's it for Decoding: Temperature, Top-k, Top-p. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
